questions.stem: A country has an absolute advantage in producing a good when it:
options: can produce the good at a lower opportunity cost than another country
is the only country in the world with the natural resources to produce the good
exports more of the good by value than any of its trading partners
can produce more of the good than another country with the same resources
questions.explanation: Absolute advantage compares the output each country gets from the same quantity of resources. Producing at a lower opportunity cost is comparative advantage, a different idea.

questions.stem: The theory of absolute advantage, which argued that countries gain by specialising in what they produce most efficiently and trading, is associated with:
options: Michael Porter
John Maynard Keynes
Adam Smith
David Ricardo
questions.explanation: Adam Smith set out absolute advantage in The Wealth of Nations (1776), as part of his case against restrictions on trade. David Ricardo later developed comparative advantage, which shows gains from trade even without an absolute advantage.

questions.stem: With one day of labour, Country A can produce 8 tonnes of wheat or 4 machines, and Country B can produce 2 tonnes of wheat or 6 machines. Which statement is correct?
options: A has an absolute advantage in both wheat and machines
B has an absolute advantage in wheat and A in machines
Neither country has an absolute advantage in either good
A has an absolute advantage in wheat and B in machines
questions.explanation: A produces more wheat (8 against 2) and B more machines (6 against 4) from the same labour. Each should specialise in its own good and trade, which raises total output of both.

questions.stem: One unit of resources produces 12 tonnes of beef or 8 bolts of cloth in Australia, and 3 tonnes of beef or 6 bolts of cloth in Vietnam. Which statement is correct?
options: Australia has a comparative advantage in beef, though it has an absolute advantage in both
Australia has a comparative advantage in both goods, so trade cannot benefit either country
Vietnam has a comparative advantage in beef, as it produces fewer bolts of cloth per unit
Australia has a comparative advantage in cloth, as it produces more cloth than Vietnam does
questions.explanation: A tonne of beef costs Australia 8/12, about 0.67 bolts of cloth, but costs Vietnam 2 bolts, so Australia has the lower opportunity cost in beef. A country cannot have a comparative advantage in both goods, so Vietnam's lies in cloth.

questions.stem: In Australia one unit of resources makes 12 tonnes of beef or 8 bolts of cloth; in Vietnam it makes 3 tonnes of beef or 6 bolts of cloth. What is the opportunity cost of one bolt of cloth in Australia?
options: 0.5 tonnes of beef
2 tonnes of beef
1.5 tonnes of beef
0.67 tonnes of beef
questions.explanation: Australia gives up 12 tonnes of beef for 8 bolts of cloth, so each bolt costs 12/8 = 1.5 tonnes. In Vietnam a bolt costs only 3/6 = 0.5 tonnes, which is why Vietnam has the comparative advantage in cloth.

questions.stem: In Australia a tonne of beef costs about 0.67 bolts of cloth to produce; in Vietnam it costs 2 bolts. At which rate of exchange would both countries gain from trading Australian beef for Vietnamese cloth?
options: 1 tonne of beef for 2.5 bolts of cloth
1 tonne of beef for 3 bolts of cloth
1 tonne of beef for 1 bolt of cloth
1 tonne of beef for 0.5 bolts of cloth
questions.explanation: Both gain if the rate lies between the two opportunity costs, 0.67 and 2 bolts per tonne. At 0.5 bolts Australia would do better making its own cloth, and above 2 bolts Vietnam would do better raising its own beef.

questions.stem: David Ricardo's theory of comparative advantage showed that:
options: a country should export only the goods it produces with more output than its rivals
countries gain most from trade when they protect their industries with tariffs and quotas
trade benefits the more efficient country while the less efficient country always loses
trade can benefit both countries even when one is more efficient at producing everything
questions.explanation: Ricardo's example of England and Portugal trading cloth and wine showed that what matters is relative, not absolute, efficiency. If each country specialises where its opportunity cost is lower, total output rises and both can gain.

questions.stem: On a diagram, two countries' straight-line production possibility curves for the same two goods have different slopes. This shows that:
options: both face increasing opportunity costs, so trade would lower their total output
their resources are fully employed, so they cannot change what they produce
their opportunity costs differ, so both can gain from specialisation and trade
one country has more resources, so only the larger country can gain from trade
questions.explanation: The slope of a production possibility curve measures the opportunity cost of one good in terms of the other. Different slopes mean different opportunity costs, which is the basis for comparative advantage.

questions.stem: Specialisation and trade based on comparative advantage allow a country to:
options: consume a combination of goods outside its own production possibility curve
produce a combination of goods outside its own production possibility curve
avoid any opportunity cost when it decides what to produce at home
become self-sufficient in all the goods its residents need and want
questions.explanation: Trade does not change what a country can produce with its own resources, but swapping its specialised output at a favourable rate lets it consume beyond that limit. Production stays on or inside the curve.

questions.stem: A country's factor endowment refers to:
options: the tariffs and quotas it uses to protect its own industries
the quantity and quality of its land, labour, capital and enterprise
the total value of all the goods and services it exports in a year
the foreign investment it receives to develop new industries
questions.explanation: Factor endowment is the stock of resources a country has to work with. Australia's large endowment of minerals and farmland underpins its comparative advantage in mining and agriculture.

questions.stem: Michael Porter's 'diamond' names four determinants of national competitive advantage: factor conditions, demand conditions, related and supporting industries, and:
options: firm strategy, structure and rivalry
exchange rate and interest rate settings
tariff and quota protection from imports
absolute and comparative cost differences
questions.explanation: Porter argued in The Competitive Advantage of Nations that intense domestic rivalry pushes firms to innovate and improve, alongside the other three corners of the diamond. Protection from imports weakens rather than builds that rivalry.

questions.stem: Porter's theory of competitive advantage differs from Ricardo's comparative advantage mainly because it argues that a nation's advantage:
options: is greatest in the industries that receive the most protection
is fixed by the country's size and cannot change over time
can be created through innovation, skills and industry clusters
depends only on the natural resources a country happens to have
questions.explanation: Comparative advantage rests largely on given differences in resources and opportunity costs. Porter stressed that firms and governments can build advantage through investment in skills, research and clusters of linked firms.

questions.stem: A wine region has grape growers, barrel makers, specialist equipment suppliers and a university wine research centre close together. In Porter's diamond this best illustrates:
options: demand conditions
factor endowment of land
firm strategy and rivalry
related and supporting industries
questions.explanation: A cluster of suppliers and research institutions near an industry lowers costs and speeds the spread of new ideas. That is Porter's related and supporting industries corner, rather than the soil and climate alone.

questions.stem: Australian buyers of mining software are known for demanding reliable, advanced products, which pushes local software firms to keep improving. In Porter's diamond this is an example of:
options: related and supporting industries
government subsidies
demand conditions
factor conditions
questions.explanation: Sophisticated and demanding home buyers force firms to innovate early, which can give them an edge when they sell overseas. This is Porter's demand conditions corner.

questions.stem: The direction of Australia's trade refers to:
options: the share of trade carried by sea rather than air
the countries and regions Australia trades with
the types of goods and services Australia trades
whether Australia's exports exceed its imports
questions.explanation: Direction describes trading partners, such as China, Japan or the United States. The types of goods and services traded make up the composition of trade.

questions.stem: Over the past six decades, the direction of Australia's exports has shifted mainly:
options: away from the United States towards the Pacific Islands
away from the United Kingdom and Europe towards Asia
away from Asia towards the United Kingdom and Europe
away from New Zealand towards South America and Africa
questions.explanation: In the 1950s the United Kingdom was Australia's main export market. Japan, then China and other Asian economies, became the main buyers as they industrialised and Britain joined the European Community.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the long-term change in the composition of Australia's goods exports?
options: Services have given way to rural goods such as wool and wheat
Manufactured goods have always made up most of the total
Rural goods such as wool have given way to minerals and energy
Minerals and energy have given way to manufactured cars and machinery
questions.explanation: Wool and other rural products dominated exports in the 1950s. Today resources such as iron ore, coal and natural gas make up the largest share of goods exports, while services such as education and tourism have also grown.

questions.stem: The value of Australia's exports to a trading partner rises from $16 billion to $20 billion over a year. The percentage change is:
options: 25 per cent
20 per cent
4 per cent
125 per cent
questions.explanation: Percentage change = (new - old) / old x 100 = (20 - 16) / 16 x 100 = 25 per cent. Dividing the $4 billion rise by the new value gives 20 per cent, which uses the wrong base.

questions.stem: Australia's imports from a country fall from $48 billion to $42 billion. The percentage change is:
options: -12.0 per cent
-12.5 per cent
-14.3 per cent
-6.0 per cent
questions.explanation: Percentage change = (42 - 48) / 48 x 100 = -12.5 per cent. Dividing by the new value of 42 gives -14.3 per cent, a common error.

questions.stem: Australia sends a large share of its exports to one country. The main risk this creates is that:
options: Australia must accept that country's tariffs on all its own imports
Australian exporters lose their comparative advantage in those goods
a downturn or policy change in that country can sharply cut export income
the Australian dollar can no longer float freely against other currencies
questions.explanation: Concentrated trade links tie Australia's export income to one economy's growth and trade policy. Diversifying markets spreads that risk; it has no direct effect on whether the dollar floats.

questions.stem: Which is a disadvantage of international trade for an economy such as Australia's?
options: It prevents firms from gaining economies of scale
It raises the prices of goods that are imported
It exposes the economy to shocks in world demand and prices
It reduces the range of goods and services available to consumers
questions.explanation: Openness brings gains, but it also transmits overseas downturns and commodity price swings into the domestic economy, and import competition can cause structural unemployment. Trade widens choice and lowers import prices rather than raising them.

questions.stem: Under a fixed exchange rate system:
options: the rate is allowed to move freely within a band set by the market
the currency's value is tied to the country's terms of trade index
authorities set an official rate and buy or sell currency to hold it
the rate is set each day by demand and supply without intervention
questions.explanation: A fixed or pegged rate is set by government or the central bank, which uses its reserves of foreign currency to keep the market rate at the official level. A floating rate is determined by market demand and supply.

questions.stem: Under a floating exchange rate system, the exchange rate is determined by:
options: demand for and supply of the currency in the foreign exchange market
the central bank, which announces a new official exchange rate each quarter
the treasurer, who sets the rate in the annual federal budget
agreements between trading partners under free trade agreements
questions.explanation: In a float, the price of the currency changes continuously with market demand and supply. Australia's central bank keeps the option to intervene but does not set the rate.

questions.stem: Australia has had a floating exchange rate since:
questions.explanation: The Hawke government floated the Australian dollar in December 1983 and removed most exchange controls. Before that the dollar had been pegged, from 1976 to a trade-weighted basket of currencies under a managed system.

questions.stem: A managed exchange rate system is one in which:
options: the rate is determined only by the volume of goods a country exports
the rate moves with market forces, but authorities intervene to limit its range
the rate is fixed permanently and the central bank never buys or sells currency
the rate is set by the government's annual budget and changed once a year
questions.explanation: A managed float or crawling peg lets the currency move, but the central bank buys or sells to keep it within a target band or path. It sits between a fixed rate and a free float.

questions.stem: A government operating a fixed exchange rate officially lowers the value of its currency. This is called:
options: depreciation
revaluation
appreciation
devaluation
questions.explanation: Devaluation is a deliberate cut to an official fixed rate. Depreciation is a fall in value caused by market forces under a floating rate.

questions.stem: Under a floating exchange rate, the Reserve Bank of Australia:
options: must keep the dollar within a fixed band against the US dollar
sets the exchange rate each month to match the inflation target
may intervene occasionally to steady a disorderly or overshooting market
announces the official rate each morning and trades to hold it there
questions.explanation: The RBA does not target a level for the dollar, but it keeps discretion to buy or sell currency when the market becomes disorderly. This is rare; most of the time the market sets the rate.

questions.stem: On a demand and supply diagram for Australian dollars, a rise in the number of foreign tourists visiting Australia will:
options: shift demand to the right, so the dollar appreciates
shift supply to the right, so the dollar depreciates
shift demand to the left, so the dollar depreciates
shift supply to the left, so the dollar appreciates
questions.explanation: Foreign tourists must buy Australian dollars to spend here, which increases demand for the currency. A rightward shift in demand raises its price, an appreciation.

questions.stem: Which transaction adds to the supply of Australian dollars in the foreign exchange market?
options: A Japanese investor buying Australian government bonds
An Indian student paying fees to a Brisbane university
An Australian retailer paying for imported electronics
A Chinese steel mill paying for Australian iron ore
questions.explanation: To pay for imports, Australians sell Australian dollars to buy foreign currency, which adds to supply. The other transactions involve foreigners buying Australian dollars, adding to demand.

questions.stem: World prices for iron ore and coal fall sharply. How does a floating exchange rate help insulate the Australian economy?
options: The dollar appreciates, lowering import prices so that household spending rises to offset the fall
The exchange rate stays fixed, so exporters' income in Australian dollars is protected from the fall
The RBA must raise interest rates to defend the dollar, which reduces inflation in the economy
The dollar depreciates, cushioning exporters' income and helping other trade-exposed firms compete
questions.explanation: Lower commodity export earnings reduce demand for the dollar, so it depreciates. Each US dollar of export revenue is then worth more in Australian dollars, and other exporters and import-competing firms become more competitive, softening the downturn.

questions.stem: During a commodity price boom, the appreciation of a floating Australian dollar helps stabilise the economy mainly because it:
options: forces the RBA to cut interest rates to bring the dollar back down
lowers import prices and slows other exports, easing inflationary pressure
raises the price of imports, encouraging households to buy local goods
increases the income of every exporter, adding further to the boom
questions.explanation: A higher dollar makes imports cheaper and reduces the competitiveness of other exporters, spreading the boom's effect and restraining demand. Under a fixed rate, more of the boom would flow into domestic spending and inflation.

questions.stem: Compared with a floating rate, a disadvantage of a fixed exchange rate is that:
options: it automatically insulates the economy from falls in world commodity prices
monetary policy must be used to defend the rate rather than to manage the domestic economy
the exchange rate changes every day, making it hard for firms to plan their export prices
the central bank cannot hold any reserves of foreign currency to use in a crisis
questions.explanation: To hold a peg, a central bank may have to set interest rates to suit the exchange rate rather than domestic inflation and employment, and can run down its reserves. Daily volatility is a drawback of floating rates, not fixed ones.

questions.stem: In economics, external stability refers to:
options: low inflation and full employment within the domestic economy as a whole
a stable exchange rate fixed by the central bank
a balanced federal budget over the economic cycle
a sustainable current account balance and level of foreign liabilities
questions.explanation: External stability means Australia's dealings with the rest of the world, such as the current account and foreign debt, stay at levels that do not threaten the economy. Low inflation and full employment describe internal stability.

questions.stem: Strong growth in Australian household spending lifts employment but also draws in more imports, widening the current account deficit. This illustrates:
options: a shift in Australia's comparative advantage
a conflict between internal stability and external stability
a simultaneous improvement in both internal and external stability
trade creation under a regional trading agreement
questions.explanation: Faster domestic growth helps the internal goals of employment and growth, but rising imports weaken the external position. Trade-offs like this shape how policy responds to trade developments.

questions.stem: Foreign investment was important to Australia's mining and gas investment boom mainly because:
options: it lowered the Australian dollar, making mining exports more competitive
it reduced the primary income deficit as profits stayed in Australia
Australian saving alone could not fund the scale of new mines and gas plants
foreign investors are required by law to buy all of Australia's mineral exports
questions.explanation: Large resource projects needed far more capital than domestic saving could supply, so foreign investment filled the gap and brought technology and expertise. The capital inflow tended to raise, not lower, the dollar.

questions.stem: A drawback of relying on foreign direct investment to develop resource projects is that:
options: foreign investment reduces the capital available for the projects
it automatically creates a surplus on the current account
profits are later paid to foreign owners, adding to the primary income deficit
the projects are not allowed to export their output while foreign owners hold shares
questions.explanation: Foreign-owned projects send dividends and profits overseas once they are running, which are debits in the primary income account. That is the cost of using foreign rather than domestic saving.

questions.stem: A sustained appreciation of the Australian dollar is most likely to reduce employment in:
options: non-traded services such as hairdressing and local cafes
firms that import most of their inputs and sell only in Australia
industries whose output is protected by import quotas
trade-exposed industries such as tourism, education and manufacturing
questions.explanation: A higher dollar makes Australian exports dearer for foreigners and imports cheaper for locals, so firms competing in world markets lose sales. Non-traded services are largely sheltered from exchange rate movements.

questions.stem: Economic integration between countries is best described as:
options: transferring all trade decisions to the International Monetary Fund
reducing barriers to trade and linking economic policies between them
each country producing all its own goods to avoid relying on others
fixing each country's exchange rate at the same official level
questions.explanation: Integration ranges from free trade areas, which remove tariffs among members, to economic unions, which share a market, harmonise policies and sometimes a currency. It is the opposite of self-sufficiency.
